entityDossier.whatItIs: Volume II of the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office's Report on the Historical Record of U.S. Government Involvement with Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena — the sequel that Volume I (cleared for public release March 2024) explicitly promised. As of August 2026 no Volume II has been published, and AARO has also not issued its 2025 annual report. The entity is therefore a documented promise and a documented non-delivery rather than a document.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: Volume I did not close its own investigation; it closed the public phase of it. AARO named a Department of Homeland Security prospective special access program (KONA BLUE), disclosed that an Intelligence Community Controlled Access Program had its scope expanded in 2021 "to protect UAP reverse-engineering" and was then disestablished, and asserted that every alleged reverse-engineering program it examined either did not exist, was a misidentified authentic sensitive program, or resolved to "an unwarranted and disestablished program." Each of those three outcomes is an admission that named, real, compartmented activity exists behind the denial. Volume I then deferred everything unresolved to a Volume II that never came. The non-publication is the finding: the office that was granted, by its own account, "full, unrestricted access by all organizations" produced one volume of conclusions and no volume of the remaining work. A promised second volume that never appears converts a partial exculpation into a permanent one, because there is no dated deliverable against which anyone can measure what was left out.
entityDossier.narrative:
The statutory hook is Section 6802 of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023 (Public Law 117-263, enacted 23 December 2022), which rewrote the 2021 UAP framework, codified much of it at 50 U.S.C. 3373, and directed AARO to conduct a historical review of all U.S. Government UAP activity from 1 January 1945 forward, reporting no later than 540 days after enactment — roughly 15 June 2024. The statute reached the exact material a legacy program would generate: any program or activity protected by restricted access that had not been explicitly and clearly reported to Congress, and any efforts to obfuscate, manipulate public opinion, hide, or otherwise provide incorrect information about UAP. Congress also directed the Comptroller General to monitor the review's progress and brief designated members.

AARO answered in March 2024 with a document titled Volume I. The title itself is the tell. A single report was due; AARO delivered a first installment, front-loaded the conclusions, and moved the unfinished work into a second installment. Volume I states that AARO "remains open to additional, verifiable information that may alter the conclusions rendered in Volume I and will note any changes to the findings in this report in Volume II," and elsewhere commits to publishing Volume II in accordance with the Section 6802 date while confining it to information acquired after Volume I's publication. That construction is load-bearing: the statutory deadline is satisfied by Volume I, and Volume II inherits no independent enforceable date of its own. Nothing in the record obliges anyone to produce it, and nobody has.

What Volume I left on the table is specific. AARO disclosed KONA BLUE, a UAP-related Prospective Special Access Program pitched to DHS and "supported by individuals who believed the USG was hiding off-world technology," which DHS never approved. It disclosed that in 2021, "without sufficient justification, the scope of an IC Controlled Access Program was expanded to protect UAP reverse-engineering," and that the program "was disestablished due to its lack of merit." AARO does not name the IC program, does not name the original classification authority that expanded it, does not say who requested the expansion, and does not say what the program's pre-2021 scope was. It disclosed a materials analysis resolving a sample to magnesium "and bismuth with some other trace elements, such as lead," based on materials characterization. It attributed the reverse-engineering allegations to "circular reporting from a group of individuals" who "have been involved in various UAP-related endeavors since at least 2009," and tied many of them to "a cancelled DIA program and the subsequent but failed attempt to reestablish this program under DHS, called KONA BLUE" — an unmistakable reference to AAWSAP/BAASS and the Bigelow-Puthoff-Davis network, named by function rather than by name.

Every one of those threads is a live investigative lead, and each was left dangling. Who inside the IC expanded a Controlled Access Program to cover reverse-engineering in 2021, and on what asserted basis, is exactly the question Congress wrote Section 6802 to answer. AARO's own framing concedes that at least one compartment did, for some period, formally exist to protect UAP reverse-engineering. Whether it protected a real capability or a phantom, someone signed the security classification guide.

The delivery record since then is thin. DefenseScoop reported on 25 February 2026 that AARO had published neither its 2025 annual report nor a second volume of the historical review, while its caseload exceeded 2,000 cases. The FY2026 NDAA (P.L. 119-60, signed 18 December 2025) added three new AARO obligations — NORTHCOM/NORAD intercept briefings, an accounting of UAP-related security classification guides, and consolidation of duplicative reporting — but did not compel Volume II. Congress layered new demands on top of an unfulfilled old one without noticing, or without minding, that the old one had lapsed.

Read as an artifact of the concealment effort, Volume I is an unusually well-executed document. It is signed, dated, sourced, and comprehensive in tone; it names two compartmented programs, concedes access to a third, and asserts that AARO went everywhere and found nothing. Its most consequential feature is structural rather than substantive: by splitting the report, AARO produced an authoritative-sounding public verdict while retaining the ability never to publish the working papers behind it. Two and a half years on, that is precisely what has happened.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026, S. 2296 of the 119th Congress, signed into law on 18 December 2025 as Public Law 119-60. It carries three UAP-related provisions affecting AARO. It does not carry the UAP Disclosure Act, which was excluded for the third consecutive year.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The FY2026 NDAA is the clearest available measurement of what Congress can and cannot pass on this subject. What survived is procedural: briefings, an inventory of classification guides, and reporting consolidation. What died — again — was every provision with teeth: records preservation, an independent Review Board, eminent domain over privately held recovered material, and mandatory declassification timelines. The pattern is now three cycles deep and consistent in kind: the disclosure architecture is introduced in the Senate with bipartisan leadership sponsorship, and it is removed in or around conference. One surviving provision is unusually revealing on its own terms — a directive that AARO account for the UAP-related security classification guides governing its own reports and investigations. A classification guide is a written instrument with an author, a date, and an original classification authority. Congress asking for an inventory of them is Congress conceding it does not know how many exist or who wrote them.
entityDossier.narrative:
S. 2296 passed the Senate on 10 October 2025 and became P.L. 119-60 on 18 December 2025. Three UAP provisions made the conferenced text, all of them modifications to the existing AARO framework rather than new authorities.

The first amends the AARO mandate to require the director to supply Congress with briefings and data on UAP intercepts conducted by U.S. Northern Command and the North American Aerospace Defense Command going back to 2004 — specifically the "number, location, and nature" of such intercepts, together with the procedures and protocols followed, "including any data collected or analyzed during such intercepts." The 2004 start date is not arbitrary; it is the year of the USS Nimitz/USS Princeton encounters off southern California. That a statutory obligation was needed in 2025 to get NORTHCOM and NORAD intercept data in front of Congress establishes that, for twenty-one years, the commands responsible for defending North American airspace were not routinely providing it — not to Congress, not to AARO, and not to the scientific community. Christopher Mellon, the former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence who now chairs the Disclosure Foundation's board, has made precisely that point publicly: the United States operates some of the world's most advanced sensor systems, and what those systems capture about anomalous incursions has not been reaching oversight.

The second provision directs AARO to account for the UAP-related security classification guides that apply to information used in reports and investigations of the phenomena. This is the provision an analyst should mine. Security classification guides are the operative documents of concealment: they are what tells a program office which facts are classified at what level and for how long, and they are signed by an original classification authority. Disclosure Foundation officials, Mellon among them, have argued in public that DoD classification guides have been applied inconsistently with executive order standards and have been used to suppress material that was previously unclassified. An accounting of those guides would produce a list of instruments, custodians and dates. Whether AARO produces it, and whether the accounting is delivered classified, is the next measurable event.

The third provision consolidates duplicative reporting requirements and streamlines how federal agencies provide data and information to the Pentagon for AARO's investigations. Streamlining is double-edged: it reduces friction for AARO, and it reduces the number of separate documents Congress receives.

Against that, consider what was excluded. Rep. Eric Burlison (R-MO) submitted the UAP Disclosure Act of 2025 as an amendment to the FY2026 NDAA in late August 2025. It would have prohibited the destruction or alteration of UAP records, created a UAP Records Collection at the National Archives, established an independent UAP Records Review Board, and required public disclosure of UAP records within twenty-five years absent a presidential certification of a clear national security reason for delay. It failed in the House. On the Senate side the same architecture was offered as S.Amdt. 3111 to S. 2296. Neither survived. The UAP Disclosure Act has now been excluded from three consecutive defense authorization bills despite bipartisan Senate backing associated with Schumer, Rounds and Gillibrand, and Liberation Times has reported that sources attribute the FY2026 failure specifically to Senator Mitch McConnell.

The records-destruction prohibition is the provision whose repeated exclusion should be read hardest. It is cheap, non-controversial on its face, and imposes no disclosure burden — it merely freezes the evidentiary record in place. Its removal, three cycles running, from a bill that Congress has enacted for more than six decades without fail, is a fact about the removers. The precedent for why it matters is documentary and sixty years old: GAO found in 1995 that the administrative records and outgoing message traffic of Roswell Army Air Field for the relevant period were destroyed with no indication of by whom or under what authority (see gao-nsiad-95-187). A statutory bar on destruction is the one measure that would prevent the 1995 finding from recurring, and it is the measure that keeps not passing.

Jordan Flowers, executive director of the Disclosure Foundation — the rebranded UAP Disclosure Fund — characterized the three enacted provisions as "a meaningful, if incremental, step toward transparency and oversight," and noted that two of them mirror recommendations Mellon and his team had promoted for years. That is the accurate reading: the FY2026 NDAA moved the oversight perimeter a few feet and left the custody question untouched.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The contractor turn-in provision of the Fiscal Year 2024 Intelligence Authorization Act: a Gillibrand amendment adopted unanimously by the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence on 14 June 2023, which required any person currently or formerly under federal contract holding government-derived UAP material to notify AARO within 60 days and, within 180 days, to hand over "a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material" for assessment, analysis and inspection. It carried a safe harbor, a sweeping funding ban on unreported UAP special access programs, and a Sense of Congress. It was numbered Sec. 1104 in S. 2103 as reported on 22 June 2023, renumbered as the bill moved, and was enacted in drastically narrowed form as Section 7343 of Division G of P.L. 118-31 on 22 December 2023.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the single most important statutory hook on the board because it is the only text Congress has ever voted out of committee that presumes, on its face, that private contractors are holding non-earth-origin material derived from federal programs and that treats getting it back as an administrative problem with a deadline. A safe harbor is not written for a hypothetical. Congress does not draft immunity from criminal and civil action "for receiving" material unless someone plausibly received it. The definition of covered activities is equally load-bearing: it contemplates government or contractor personnel with "a primary, secondary, or contingency mission of capturing, recovering, and securing unidentified anomalous phenomena craft or pieces and components of such craft," and it defines the reverse-engineering perimeter as work on "any aerospace craft that uses propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust." Seventeen senators on the Intelligence Committee voted this text out. Then it was cut in conference.
entityDossier.narrative:
On 14 June 2023, nine days after The Debrief published David Grusch's allegations, the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence adopted by voice vote a UAP amendment sponsored by Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) and cosponsored by Senators Mike Rounds (R-SD), John Cornyn (R-TX) and Marco Rubio (R-FL). The committee then approved the underlying Intelligence Authorization Act unanimously. The bill was filed and numbered on 22 June 2023 as S. 2103; the UAP text appeared as Section 1104, titled "Funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena." Section 1102 of that same reported text was an unrelated provision on defense sensitive support; the board's identifier tracks a later renumbering as the IAA moved into the NDAA vehicle, and the substance — not the number — is what matters.

The operative mechanism had three parts.

First, a notification and turn-in mandate. The text reached "any person currently or formerly under contract with the Federal Government that has in their possession material or information provided by or derived from the Federal Government relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena that formerly or currently is protected by any form of special access or restricted access." Such persons had 60 days from enactment to notify the AARO director, and 180 days to provide "a comprehensive list of all non-earth origin or exotic unidentified anomalous phenomena material" in their possession and to make it available to the director for "assessment, analysis, and inspection." The AARO director then had 30 days to notify designated congressional committees and leaders of any notification, information or material received. That last clause is the accountability trigger: it would have created a dated congressional paper trail for each turn-in.

Second, a safe harbor: "No criminal or civil action may lie or be maintained in any Federal or State court against any person for receiving" the covered material or information, contingent on meeting the deadlines. Douglas Johnson, who first reported the text, read this as implying that a private entity holding non-human technology outside democratic oversight — and possibly profiting from it — would otherwise be in a legally tenuous position, and that the provision functioned as a time-limited amnesty to smooth an orderly return. Nothing in the provision created new criminal offenses, and nothing immunized threats, violence or perjury.

Third, a funding ban. No future federal funds, directly or indirectly, for any UAP-related special access program activity unless the program had been "formally, officially, explicitly, and specifically described, explained, and justified to the appropriate committees of Congress, congressional leadership, and the Director" of AARO. The designated recipients were the intelligence, armed services and appropriations committees of both chambers plus the Speaker, House minority leader, and Senate majority and minority leaders — 58 senators and 137 House members in total. The categories of covered activity were drafted in six expansive paragraphs and included recruiting, employing, training, equipping, operating and providing security for government or contractor personnel with a retrieval mission; managing and providing security for activities and information relating to UAP "from disclosure"; and reverse-engineering work reaching any aerospace craft using propulsion other than chemical propellants, solar power and electric ion thrust.

The Sense of Congress attached to the provision is the most candid language Congress has produced on the subject. It asserted that "due to the increasing potential for technology surprise from foreign adversaries and to ensure sufficient integration across the United States industrial base and avoid technology and security stovepipes... the Federal Government must expand awareness about any historical exotic technology antecedents previously provided by the Federal Government for research and development purposes." Read plainly: the government previously provided exotic technology antecedents to industry for R&D, secrecy has stovepiped that work, and the stovepiping is now a national security liability. Whether or not one accepts the premise, the drafters wrote it into a bill that a Senate committee approved unanimously.

The legislative arc from there is the concealment story in miniature. The Senate Armed Services Committee carried parallel but non-identical language at Section 1546 of S. 2226, without the safe harbor and without the Sense of Congress, and with the funding limitation confined to FY2024 DoD programs. On 20 July 2023 SSCI Chairman Mark Warner filed a revised version, SA 994, narrowing the IAA's funding limitation to FY2024 as well. The House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence approved its own FY2024 IAA (H.R. 3932) on 13 July 2023 containing no UAP provisions at all, and the House Rules Committee blocked a floor vote on Rep. Mike Gallagher's parallel amendment to the House NDAA — reportedly because of objections from HPSCI leadership, whose chairman Michael Turner and ranking member Jim Himes had made dismissive public comments about secret alien technology on 6 June 2023. The Senate passed a combined NDAA-IAA on 27 July 2023. In conference, the turn-in mandate and safe harbor did not survive. What was enacted on 22 December 2023 as Section 7343 of Division G of P.L. 118-31 is a funding limitation only, conditioned on the Director of National Intelligence providing program details to the appropriate committees and leadership — which the Intelligence chairmen explained "provides for funding limitations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena because of perceptions of insufficient transparency in this area."

The deletion is the finding. A unanimous committee wrote a hand-back-the-material provision with an amnesty clause, and the amnesty and the hand-back both vanished behind closed doors.

entityDossier.whatItIs: EarthTech International, Inc. is a private research company in Austin, Texas, incorporated in 1991 as the corporate vehicle for the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin, which Harold E. Puthoff founded in 1985. Its declared research program covers spacetime and gravitation theory, the quantum vacuum and zero-point energy, modifications to standard electrodynamics, interstellar flight science, and SETI, framed as inputs to innovative space propulsion and energy generation. Puthoff is president, CEO and board chairman; Eric W. Davis is chief science officer.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: EarthTech is the intellectual clearinghouse where the legacy program's technical vocabulary was written down and then sold back to the government as reference literature. Under the Defense Intelligence Agency's Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program, EarthTech was subcontracted through Robert Bigelow's BAASS, and Puthoff and Davis commissioned the set of expert studies that DIA published as Defense Intelligence Reference Documents on traversable wormholes, antigravity, metamaterials and invisibility cloaking. That output supplied the exact conceptual frame — non-chemical propulsion, spacetime metric engineering, exotic materials — that Congress later wrote into statute as the boundary of a covered reverse-engineering program. AARO's Historical Record Report Volume I aims squarely at this network without naming it, attributing the reverse-engineering allegations to a group involved in UAP endeavors "since at least 2009" and tied to "a cancelled DIA program and the subsequent but failed attempt to reestablish this program under DHS, called KONA BLUE." AARO's own account therefore places these people at the center of both the DIA program and its DHS successor attempt, while insisting nothing was ever recovered.
entityDossier.narrative:
Harold E. Puthoff earned his PhD at Stanford in 1967 as a theoretical and experimental physicist working on lasers, and spent the 1970s running the SRI International parapsychology program with Russell Targ under intelligence-community sponsorship — the lineage that became Project STARGATE. In 1985 he founded the Institute for Advanced Studies at Austin; in 1991 it was incorporated under EarthTech International, Inc. Both remain co-located in Austin. Eric W. Davis, whose declared specializations include breakthrough propulsion physics, beamed energy propulsion, directed energy weapons, general relativity, quantum field theory, quantum gravity and what he calls SETI-xenoarchaeology, is chief science officer of both entities.

The institutional significance is not the physics. It is that EarthTech occupied, for four decades, a specific structural position: a small, privately held, security-cleared research house with no shareholders to answer to, no publication obligations, and a standing relationship with the parts of the defense and intelligence enterprise that buy speculative propulsion analysis. That is precisely the shape of entity a legacy program would need — small enough to compartment, technical enough to be credible, private enough to sit outside the FOIA perimeter.

The documented engagement is AAWSAP. In 2008 the Defense Intelligence Agency awarded a contract to Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, reported at up to $22 million over five years, to assess advanced aerospace threats. Puthoff served as the program's chief scientist on the BAASS side, and EarthTech was subcontracted to produce the written product. Puthoff and Davis commissioned a series of thirty-eight expert studies, which DIA then issued as Defense Intelligence Reference Documents. The subjects released into the public record include traversable wormholes and negative energy, antigravity, metamaterials for aerospace applications, and invisibility cloaking. Whatever one makes of the science, the procurement fact is unambiguous: a U.S. intelligence agency paid, through a contractor and a subcontractor, for a reference library on how one would build and analyze a craft that violates the propulsion assumptions of every acquisition program in the department. Fifteen years later Congress drafted the covered-activity definition for UAP reverse-engineering as any aerospace craft using "propulsion technology other than chemical propellants, solar power, and electric ion thrust" — the DIRD library's subject matter, rendered as statutory text.

Davis is also the pivot of the two most consequential unofficial documents in the modern record. In October 2002 he met with retired Vice Admiral Thomas Ray Wilson, former director of DIA; the handwritten notes of that conversation, describing a special access program under contractor control that had denied access to a senior flag officer, surfaced publicly in 2019 as the Wilson-Davis memo. In July 2020 the New York Times reported that Davis, then a contractor for Aerospace Corporation, had briefed a Defense Department agency in October 2019 and Senate Armed Services Committee staff about retrievals from "off-world vehicles not made on this earth." Both items are contested; neither is invented. Both were produced by the chief science officer of EarthTech International.

The AARO response is where this entity becomes central rather than peripheral. Volume I never names EarthTech, Puthoff, Davis or Bigelow. It does not need to. It states that the modern reverse-engineering claims stem "largely" from "a consistent group of individuals who have been involved in various UAP-related endeavors since at least 2009," and that many of them were "involved in or supportive of a cancelled DIA program and the subsequent but failed attempt to reestablish this program under DHS, called KONA BLUE." The cancelled DIA program is AAWSAP. AARO's rebuttal is therefore built on the same population that AARO concedes staffed a real, funded DIA program and then attempted, unsuccessfully, to stand up a DHS prospective special access program to continue it. AARO also reports resolving a claimed anomalous material sample to magnesium "and bismuth with some other trace elements, such as lead" by materials characterization — the layered magnesium-bismuth specimen that has circulated through this network for decades and been analyzed by parties associated with it.

The network extends forward. Davis appears on the team roster of the Disclosure Foundation, the organization chaired by former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Intelligence Christopher Mellon, whose published recommendations two of the three FY2026 NDAA UAP provisions mirror. So the same technical population that wrote the DIA reference library, that AARO identifies as the source of the circular reporting, and that pitched KONA BLUE to DHS, is also inside the advocacy apparatus that now shapes what Congress writes into the defense authorization act. That is not a contradiction. It is what a closed technical community looks like when the subject matter has no other constituency.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The RAND Corporation is a nonprofit research institution created by the U.S. Army Air Forces in 1946 as Project RAND, operating under contract to the Douglas Aircraft Company, and spun out as an independent California nonprofit in 1948 with initial capital from the Ford Foundation. It operates federally funded research and development centers for the Department of Defense, including Project AIR FORCE, the National Defense Research Institute and the Army Research Division, and has published on unidentified aerial phenomena in both 1968 and 2023.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: RAND is the original defense-contractor-adjacent think tank, born inside an airframe manufacturer and chartered to think about things the Air Force could not think about in uniform. It sat at the center of the 1946-1968 window in which any recovery and exploitation effort would have needed exactly RAND's product: threat framing, capability assessment, and analytic cover. Its 1968 internal draft "UFOs: What To Do?" states flatly that the phenomenon is "unambiguously extraordinary and clearly inexplicable in modern terms" — a judgment produced inside the Air Force's own analytic arm during the same period the Condon Committee was preparing to declare the subject scientifically barren. RAND stamped that document for internal use only and reportedly refused to acknowledge its existence for thirty-two years. Fifty-five years later, RAND published an OSD-sponsored study whose central finding is that public UAP reports cluster around military operations areas — analytically useful, and also the most institutionally comfortable finding available, since it relocates the phenomenon inside U.S. military activity without ever addressing recovery or custody.
entityDossier.narrative:
Project RAND was created in 1946 under contract between the Army Air Forces and the Douglas Aircraft Company, expressly to retain the civilian scientific talent that had won the war. Its first assignment, delivered on a three-week deadline, was the design of a world-circling spaceship; the resulting "Preliminary Design of an Experimental World-Circling Spaceship" was released in May 1946. The organization incorporated as a California nonprofit on 14 May 1948, and on 1 November 1948 the Project RAND contract was formally transferred from Douglas Aircraft to the RAND Corporation, with the Ford Foundation supplying the initial capital for the spin-off.

That founding sequence is the point. RAND was a defense contractor's internal analysis shop that became a national institution by changing its corporate wrapper without changing its customer. The July 1947 Roswell events fall squarely inside the Douglas-contract period; the FBI teletype GAO later recovered records that the recovered disc and balloon were "being sent to Wright Field... for examination" — Wright Field being Air Materiel Command, the same enterprise for which Project RAND was doing its earliest work on exotic aerospace concepts. GAO in 1995 could find no Air Materiel Command records from 1947-1950 mentioning the crash or any examination of debris.

RAND's documented engagement with the phenomenon comes in two widely separated bursts.

The first is DRU-1571, "UFOs: What To Do?", by George Kocher, 1968, forty-three pages. RAND's own abstract for the document is unusually direct: "Since World War II, however, there seems to have been a drastic increase in the number of sightings. We have enough data — both visual and photographic — on some of these sightings to know that the phenomenon is unambiguously extraordinary and clearly inexplicable in modern terms." Kocher examines UFO brightness, size and maneuvers, discusses the frequency and location of sightings, and closes by proposing standardized reporting so that times and locations of appearances may be anticipated and objective data obtained. He recommended going beyond a national collection to worldwide data with intensive investigation of the most interesting reports. The document is dated 27 November 1968 and was stamped for RAND use only, with instructions not to quote or cite externally; researchers report that RAND did not acknowledge the paper's existence and authenticity until 2000. RAND now files it in a series it describes as unrestricted drafts that "were not usually formally edited or peer reviewed" — a retrospective classification that softens a document written by its own staff during the exact months the Air Force was preparing to shut down Project Blue Book on the strength of the Condon report.

The timing is the finding. In late 1968 the Air Force's analytic contractor produced an internal paper saying the phenomenon was real, extraordinary and inexplicable, and recommending a global standardized collection architecture. In January 1969 the Condon report was released and Blue Book was terminated. The Kocher draft was suppressed for a generation.

The second burst is 2023. RAND published "Not the X-Files: Mapping Public Reports of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Across America," report number RR-A2475-1, by Marek N. Posard, Ashley Gromis and Mary Lee. The research was sponsored by the Office of the Secretary of Defense and conducted within the Acquisition and Technology Policy Program of the RAND National Security Research Division. The authors analyzed 101,151 public UAP reports across 12,783 U.S. Census Bureau locations. The headline result is that reports cluster near Military Operations Areas — designated blocks of airspace for military training and maneuvering, not necessarily near airbases. RAND completed the report in May 2023, sent it to the Department of Defense for review, and published it on 25 July 2023 — the day before the House Oversight Committee's UAP hearing at which David Grusch testified.

For an analyst, the 2023 study is a two-edged artifact. Its finding is genuinely useful: whatever is being reported, it is being reported disproportionately where the military flies. That is consistent with misidentification of military activity, and it is equally consistent with the phenomenon exhibiting interest in military activity — the correlation does not discriminate. What the study does not do, and was not scoped to do, is ask a single question about recovery, custody, materials, or program structure. An OSD-sponsored study, reviewed by the Department before release, published the day before the most consequential UAP hearing in fifty years, framing the entire subject as a geography-of-misidentification problem, is exactly the deliverable a concealment posture would commission. That does not make the analysis wrong. It makes the timing and the scoping evidence about the sponsor.

RAND's structural position remains what it was in 1946: an FFRDC operator with continuous classified access across Project AIR FORCE, the National Defense Research Institute and the Army Research Division, publishing an unclassified fraction of its output and disclaiming that its publications "do not necessarily reflect the opinions of its research clients and sponsors." Between 1968 and 2023 the public record shows nothing. Fifty-five years of an FFRDC's silence on a subject its own analyst called unambiguously extraordinary is itself a data point.

RAND's own abstract for DRU-1571 states: "We have enough data—both visual and photographic—on some of these sightings to know that the phenomenon is unambiguously extraordinary and clearly inexplicable in modern terms."

Kocher's paper examines UFO brightness, size and maneuvers, discusses the frequency and location of sightings, and concludes by proposing standardized reporting so that times and locations of appearances may be anticipated and objective data obtained.
RAND characterizes the drafts series containing DRU-1571 as unrestricted drafts that, although approved for circulation, "were not usually formally edited or peer reviewed."

The Kocher document was dated 27 November 1968 and stamped "For RAND Use Only" with instructions not to quote or cite it in external publications; RAND is reported to have declined to acknowledge the paper's existence and authenticity until 2000.
RAND published "Not the X-Files: Mapping Public Reports of Unidentified Aerial Phenomena Across America," report RR-A2475-1, by Marek N. Posard, Ashley Gromis and Mary Lee.
The 2023 RAND UAP study was sponsored by the Office of the Secretary of Defense and conducted within the Acquisition and Technology Policy Program of the RAND National Security Research Division.
The study presented a geographic analysis of 101,151 public reports of UAP sightings across 12,783 U.S. Census Bureau locations.

The study's principal finding is that unknown aircraft are most commonly reported near Military Operations Areas — blocks of airspace designated for military practice and maneuvering, which are not necessarily near air bases.
claims.source: Popular Science, "The connection between UAP reports and Military Operations Areas," https://www.popsci.com/technology/rand-report-uap-military-operations-areas/

claims.text: RAND completed the report in May 2023, sent it to the Department of Defense for review, and published it on 25 July 2023 — the day before the House Oversight Committee's 26 July 2023 UAP hearing.

RAND operates federally funded research and development centers for the Department of Defense through Project AIR FORCE, the National Defense Research Institute, and the RAND Army Research Division (Arroyo Center).

The Department of the Air Force's first transfer into NARA Record Group 615 (series 656595571, 30 items, accessioned 28 August 2026) contains two RAND items sixteen years apart: item 342UAP00003, the Curtis LeMay Collection 1945-1947, which carries a 5 August 1947 report naming Project RAND; and item 342UAP00025, RAND Memorandum RM-3178-PR of March 1963.

A report headed 'Report on Evaluation of Military Worth Activities (Reports Control Symbol WDCSO-(OT)-50)', Operations Analysis AC/AS-3, dated 5 August 1947 and directed to the Deputy Chief of Air Staff for Research and Development, states that "The principal AAF activity in this particular field is Project RAND (AAF Project MX-791)."

The same 5 August 1947 report gives estimated man-days of work performed on Project RAND during June 1947 as: military personnel 30, civilian 10, contractor's personnel RAND proper 2,200 and RAND subcontractors 1,400, total 3,600 -- so contractor effort was roughly ninety times government effort at the point RAND was still inside Douglas Aircraft.

Item 342UAP00025 of the Air Force RG 615 transfer is RAND Memorandum RM-3178-PR, "A Survey of Exobiology" by Paul G. Seybold, March 1963, marked UNCLASSIFIED and "PREPARED FOR: UNITED STATES AIR FORCE PROJECT RAND", bearing an Aerospace Studies Institute Archives Branch return stamp for Maxwell AFB, Alabama.

entityDossier.denialPosture: RAND has never publicly denied anything about UAP; its posture is non-engagement punctuated by two publications fifty-five years apart. The relevant artifact is the withholding: a 1968 internal paper by a RAND analyst declaring the phenomenon unambiguously extraordinary was stamped for internal use only and, per researchers who pursued it, was not acknowledged by RAND as authentic until 2000. The 2023 OSD-sponsored study restores RAND to the subject on terms that frame it entirely as a misidentification-geography problem and never touch recovery, materials or program structure.

entityDossier.whatItIs: GAO/NSIAD-95-187, B-262046, "Government Records: Results of a Search for Records Concerning the 1947 Crash Near Roswell, New Mexico" — a General Accounting Office letter report issued 28 July 1995 to Representative Steven H. Schiff of New Mexico. It documents a fifteen-month government-wide search for records on the Roswell events, conducted March 1994 to June 1995 across NARA, the National Personnel Records Center, the FBI, CIA, NSA, DoD, DOE, the National Security Council and the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: This is the single strongest tier-one document on the board, because it is a congressional audit agency reporting, in its own voice and under its own signature, that the primary records of the unit at the center of the founding incident were destroyed and that nobody can say who destroyed them or under what authority. GAO found the administrative records of Roswell Army Air Field for March 1945 through December 1949 and its outgoing message traffic for October 1946 through December 1949 gone, with a disposition form that "does not indicate what organization or person destroyed the records and when or under what authority the records were destroyed." It found that in 1947 Army regulations required air accident reports to be maintained permanently. It found no regulation governing the handling of the debris the FBI recorded as en route to Wright Field, and no Air Materiel Command record of that debris ever arriving or being examined. It found the records of the 1395th Military Police Company (Aviation) — the security unit — never retired to the records center at all. Every element of a documentary cover is present in a 1995 GAO letter report, and it has been sitting in the public record for thirty-one years.
entityDossier.narrative:
Representative Steven H. Schiff (R-NM) asked GAO for this work because, in GAO's own framing, he was "Concerned that the Department of Defense (DOD) may not have provided you with all available information on the crash." That sentence, in a GAO letter report, is a member of Congress on the record stating that he did not believe the Pentagon's answers about Roswell. GAO's mandate was narrow — determine the reporting requirements for air accidents like the Roswell crash, and identify any government records concerning it — and GAO answered both.

On requirements: "In 1947, Army regulations required that air accident reports be maintained permanently." GAO identified four air accidents reported by the Army Air Forces in New Mexico during July 1947, all involving military fighter or cargo aircraft, and all occurring after 8 July 1947 — the date the RAAF public information office announced the recovery of a flying disc. The Navy reported none. Air Force officials told GAO that under the record-keeping requirements then in effect, there was no requirement to prepare a report on the crash of a weather balloon. That is the pivot on which the official account rests: reclassify the object as a balloon and the permanent-retention requirement evaporates.

On records: GAO went to the National Personnel Records Center in St. Louis and obtained documentation showing that RAAF administrative records covering finance and accounting, supplies, buildings and grounds and other general administrative matters from March 1945 through December 1949, and RAAF outgoing messages from October 1946 through December 1949, were destroyed. GAO's finding on authority is stated twice, in two forms, and both are unambiguous. In Results in Brief: "The document disposition form does not indicate what organization or person destroyed the records and when or under what authority the records were destroyed." In the body, attributed to the Center's Chief Archivist: "the document disposition form did not properly indicate the authority under which the disposal action was taken." The Chief Archivist added, from personal experience, "that many of the Air Force organizational records covering this time period were destroyed without entering a citation for the governing disposition authority," and GAO's own review of records control forms for other destroyed material — including outgoing RAAF messages for 1950 — supported that view.

That last detail deserves an analyst's attention, because it cuts both ways and should be handled honestly. GAO and the Chief Archivist offer a systemic explanation: sloppy Air Force records management across the whole period, not targeted destruction. But a systemic practice of destroying records without citing disposition authority is precisely the environment in which a targeted destruction becomes undetectable. GAO does not, and cannot, distinguish between the two. The report establishes that the records are gone and that the paper trail for their destruction is defective. It does not establish intent, and it does not need to for the record to be load-bearing.

GAO further reports that document disposition forms show the Walker Air Force Base records officer transferred unit histories to the Army's Kansas City depository in 1953 — the 509th Bomb Group and RAAF for February to October 1947, the 1st Air Transport Unit for July 1946 to June 1947, the 427th Army Air Force Base Unit for January 1946 to February 1947. But: "We could not locate any documentation indicating that records of the 1395th Military Police Company (Aviation) were ever retired to the National Personnel Records Center or its predecessor depositories." The military police company at the field where the recovery was announced has no retirement record at all.

GAO's entire yield from 1947 was two documents. The July 1947 combined 509th Bomb Group/RAAF history states the public information office "was kept quite busy . . . answering inquiries on the 'flying disc,' which was reported to be in [the] possession of the 509th Bomb Group. The object turned out to be a radar tracking balloon," certified by the commanding officer's signature as a complete and accurate account. And an FBI teletype of 8 July 1947 from the Dallas field office reporting that an Eighth Air Force headquarters official had telephonically advised of the recovery near Roswell of "a hexagonal-shaped disc suspended from a large balloon by cable," that the recovered object resembled a high-altitude weather balloon with a radar reflector, and that "the disc and balloon were being sent to Wright Field . . . for examination." The FBI conducted no further investigation.

GAO then followed the debris. "Because the FBI message reported that debris from the Roswell crash was being transported to Wright Field for examination, we attempted to determine whether military regulations existed for handling such debris. We were unable to locate any applicable regulation." And: GAO reviewed Air Materiel Command records from 1947 to 1950 and "found no records mentioning the Roswell crash or the examination by Air Materiel Command personnel of any debris recovered from the crash." Material was documented as shipped to Wright Field. There is no governing regulation for how such material is handled, and no record at Wright Field that it arrived, was examined, or was disposed of. That is a custody gap of exactly the shape a legacy program requires at its origin.

The agency responses complete the picture. The NSC, OSTP and Department of Energy said they held nothing. DoD said the July 1994 Air Force Roswell report was the extent of its records, and offered no comments on GAO's draft. The CIA's Executive Director told GAO in March 1995 that "it was unclear whether the CIA had ever conducted a search for records specifically relating to Roswell" — forty-eight years after the event — and then ordered one; on 30 May 1995 he reported no documents. GAO's methodology section concedes the environment: "Our search of government records was complicated by the fact that some records we wanted to review were missing and there was not always an explanation."

claims.text: GAO states the request originated because Rep. Schiff was "Concerned that the Department of Defense (DOD) may not have provided you with all available information on the crash."
GAO found that RAAF administrative records from March 1945 through December 1949 and RAAF outgoing messages from October 1946 through December 1949 were destroyed.
GAO states: "The document disposition form does not indicate what organization or person destroyed the records and when or under what authority the records were destroyed."

The Chief Archivist of the National Personnel Records Center told GAO that "the document disposition form did not properly indicate the authority under which the disposal action was taken," and that from his personal experience "many of the Air Force organizational records covering this time period were destroyed without entering a citation for the governing disposition authority."

GAO states: "In 1947, Army regulations required that air accident reports be maintained permanently." Air Force officials told GAO there was no requirement to prepare a report on the crash of a weather balloon.

GAO identified four Army Air Forces air accidents in New Mexico during July 1947, all involving military fighter or cargo aircraft and all occurring after 8 July 1947, at or near Hobbs, Albuquerque, Carrizozo and Alamogordo; the Navy reported none.

GAO "could not locate any documentation indicating that records of the 1395th Military Police Company (Aviation) were ever retired to the National Personnel Records Center or its predecessor depositories," although 1953 disposition forms show the Walker AFB records officer transferred the histories of the 509th Bomb Group/RAAF, the 1st Air Transport Unit and the 427th Army Air Force Base Unit to the Army's Kansas City depository.

The July 1947 combined 509th Bomb Group and RAAF history states the RAAF public information office "was kept quite busy . . . answering inquiries on the 'flying disc,' which was reported to be in [the] possession of the 509th Bomb Group. The object turned out to be a radar tracking balloon," certified by the commanding officer's signature as a complete and accurate account of RAAF activities in July 1947.

The FBI teletype of 8 July 1947 from the Dallas office recorded that an Eighth Air Force headquarters official telephonically reported the recovery near Roswell of "a hexagonal-shaped disc suspended from a large balloon by cable," and that "the disc and balloon were being sent to Wright Field . . . for examination"; the FBI conducted no further investigation.
GAO states: "we attempted to determine whether military regulations existed for handling such debris. We were unable to locate any applicable regulation."

GAO reviewed Air Materiel Command (Wright Field) records from 1947 to 1950 and "found no records mentioning the Roswell crash or the examination by Air Materiel Command personnel of any debris recovered from the crash."

In March 1995 the CIA's Executive Director told GAO that it was "unclear whether the CIA had ever conducted a search for records specifically relating to Roswell," then directed a comprehensive search; on 30 May 1995 he reported that a search of the term "Roswell, New Mexico" across all CIA databases produced no documents related to the crash.

DoD told GAO that the July 1994 Report of Air Force Research Regarding the Roswell Incident represented the extent of DoD records or information on the crash, and DoD "offered no comments or suggested changes to the report" when given GAO's draft. GAO's methodology section states: "Our search of government records was complicated by the fact that some records we wanted to review were missing and there was not always an explanation."

entityDossier.denialPosture: The Department of Defense's position, recorded in GAO's report, is that the July 1994 Report of Air Force Research Regarding the Roswell Incident — attributing the debris to a Project MOGUL balloon train — constitutes the entirety of the department's records and information on the subject, and DoD declined to comment on GAO's draft at all. The Air Force's 1994 report did not dispute that something happened near Roswell. The National Security Council, the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy and the Department of Energy each certified they held nothing. The CIA's denial is the most revealing: forty-eight years after the event its own Executive Director could not confirm that any Roswell-specific records search had ever been performed.
connections: Rep. Steven H. Schiff (R-NM) — requester; the member who told GAO in writing that he doubted DoD had given him everything. Schiff died in 1998.
Richard Davis, GAO Director, National Security Analysis, and Gary K. Weeter, Assistant Director — the named GAO officials responsible for the report.

Roswell Army Air Field / Walker Air Force Base, 509th Bomb Group, 1st Air Transport Unit, 427th AAF Base Unit, 1395th Military Police Company (Aviation) — the units whose records were destroyed, transferred, or never retired.

Wright Field / Air Materiel Command (later Wright-Patterson AFB) — documented destination of the recovered disc and balloon per the FBI teletype, with no corresponding receipt or examination record 1947-1950. The historical anchor for every subsequent claim about Wright-Patterson as a custody node.
Eighth Air Force headquarters, Fort Worth — source of the telephonic report to the FBI and of the same-day balloon retraction.
FBI Dallas and Cincinnati field offices — originator and addressee of the only surviving contemporaneous federal record outside the unit history.
Project MOGUL — the classified balloon program invoked in the Air Force's 1994 report as the explanation.
National Personnel Records Center, St. Louis — custodian of the disposition forms that fail to cite destruction authority.
ndaa-fy2026 — the records-destruction prohibition repeatedly stripped from the UAP Disclosure Act is the direct legislative remedy for the condition GAO documented in 1995.
aaro-historical-record-vol2 — AARO's Section 6802 historical review covers 1 January 1945 forward, i.e., the same period whose primary records GAO found destroyed.
openQuestions: Who destroyed the RAAF administrative records and outgoing messages, when, and under what claimed authority — the disposition form does not say and GAO could not determine it.
Whether the 1395th Military Police Company (Aviation) records were destroyed, misfiled, retained elsewhere, or never created; GAO found no retirement documentation of any kind.
Whether any Air Materiel Command receiving record for the shipment described in the 8 July 1947 FBI teletype exists in any classification or in any non-AMC file series.
Why no military regulation governed the handling of recovered airborne debris in 1947, and whether a classified handling instruction existed outside the regulation system.
What the Eighth Air Force official's name was, and whether the FBI's Dallas office recorded it; GAO does not name him.
Whether GAO's underlying working papers for NSIAD-95-187 survive and are obtainable, including the classified documents GAO says it examined.
Whether Rep. Schiff received any classified supplement or briefing beyond the public letter report.

Whether the systemic non-citation of disposition authority the Chief Archivist described is documented anywhere as an Air Force records-management finding, or whether it exists only as his personal characterization to GAO.
